A few threads run through my work: get messy biomedical data into a form people
can analyze, write open-source software so others can do the same, and check
that the methods hold up. Below are the projects I'm working on now, the papers
I'd point someone to first, and the repositories I find most useful. Everything
else is on the [Software](software.qmd) and [Publications](publications.qmd)
pages and on [GitHub](https://github.com/muschellij2).

## Accelerometry & wearables {#accelerometry}

Most of my current work is on wrist-worn accelerometers: turning raw,
sub-second data into steps, sleep, non-wear, and activity measures that can be
compared across devices and studies. With the
[JHU Wearables group](https://github.com/jhuwit) I maintain a family of R
packages, collected in [activerse](https://jhuwit.github.io/activerse/), that
read data from many devices and run open-source algorithms, such as the Oxford
step-count model, directly from R. A big part of this is benchmarking: we
compare step-counting algorithms on publicly available data and in older
adults in the ARIC study.

::: {#accel-papers}
:::

::: {#accel-repos}
:::

## NHANES & population cohorts {#nhanes}

NHANES is a nationally representative US sample with wrist accelerometry, and a
lot of my time goes into making it usable. The 2011–2014 waves and the National
Youth Fitness Survey released raw 80 Hz data, which is large and awkward to
work with; [nhanes_80hz](https://github.com/muschellij2/nhanes_80hz) is the
pipeline we use to process it. We have used these data to compare
step-counting algorithms across the US population and to study physical
activity as a predictor of mortality, alongside similar work in the UK Biobank.

::: {#nhanes-papers}
:::

::: {#nhanes-repos}
:::

## Neuroimaging {#neuroimaging}

Much of my earlier work was on CT imaging of stroke: extracting the brain from
head CT and segmenting intracerebral hemorrhage. Along the way I built R
infrastructure for medical imaging, including
[Neuroconductor](https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxx068), a platform for
imaging packages in R, and interfaces such as
[fslr](https://github.com/muschellij2/fslr) and
[freesurfer](https://github.com/muschellij2/freesurfer) that let you call the
standard imaging tools from R. I still maintain these, and the CT work produced
open methods and data, including a public high-resolution CT brain template.

::: {#neuro-papers}
:::

::: {#neuro-repos}
:::

## Machine learning & AI {#ml}

Machine learning runs through all of this. For hemorrhage on CT we went from
random-forest classification of each voxel to 3D deep neural networks, and
then to Bayesian deep learning that outperformed the volume estimators used in
clinical trials. In wearables, many of the best step, activity, and sleep
models are deep-learning models written in Python; I wrap them in R so they can
be run on large cohorts and compared fairly. I also care about how models are
evaluated: ROC and AUC can mislead when the predictor is binary. More recently
I've written [opendataloader](https://github.com/muschellij2/opendataloader)
to turn PDFs into structured text from R.

::: {#ml-papers}
:::

::: {#ml-repos}
:::

## Reproducible reporting {#reproducible}

I want analyses that can be rerun and teaching materials that rebuild
themselves. [ari](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ari), the Automated R
Instructor, turns slides and a script into narrated lecture videos, so a course
can be regenerated when the material changes, and
[didactr](https://github.com/jhudsl/didactr) builds on it to automate whole
courses. Most of my papers ship with public code and data, and this site is
itself built with [Quarto](https://quarto.org) from plain data files.

::: {#repro-papers}
:::

::: {#repro-repos}
:::
